extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and policy observers interested in US immigration policy and Trump-administration controversies
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic Wikipedia article summarizing reported policies, practices, legal challenges, and individual cases relating to visa revocations, detentions, and deportations during the second Trump administration. Covers government directives, enforcement methods, court rulings, and notable detained/deported individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: INA 'adverse foreign policy' deportability standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), aliens in the U.S. may be deported if the Secretary of State believes their presence will have serious negative consequences for U.S. foreign policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes government use of this provision in cases such as Mahmoud Khalil (where the State Department asserted 'adverse foreign policy consequences'). Courts have debated its constitutionality (a district judge found it likely unconstitutional in Khalil's case; other decisions limited judicial review or required exhaustion of immigration-court remedies). The provision has historical associations with McCarthy-era practices and has been criticized as a broad, political basis for deportation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Department social-media ineligibility directive (March 25, 2025)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visa applicants would be ineligible if their social media activity indicated that they were 'advocating for, sympathizing with, or persuading others to endorse or espouse terrorist activities or support a designated foreign terrorist organization'; similar activity could result in revocation of existing visas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This directive is cited as a formal criterion used to deny or revoke visas; the article links it to the administration's 'catch and revoke' program and the large number of student visa revocations. It highlights concerns about breadth and vagueness (e.g., conflating pro‑Palestinian speech with support for terrorism) and documents that many revocations were later challenged or restored by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: DHS screening for content deemed 'antisemitic'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department of Homeland Security announced it would screen social media accounts for anything it deems 'antisemitic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a DHS screening criterion that has been used in practice to identify individuals for visa revocation or other immigration actions. The article frames this rule as controversial because of subjective interpretation and its intersection with political speech about the Gaza war and related campus protests.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEVP institutional review and potential decertification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) would review institutions of higher education that had significant pro‑Palestinian protests and could decertify those institutions, making them ineligible to enroll student visa holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an institutional-level enforcement criterion: decertification would remove an institution's ability to host international students, threatening university revenue and prompting institutions to track and contest visa revocations. The article cites trackers (Inside Higher Ed) and describes implications for colleges and their foreign-enrollment income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on viewpoint-discriminatory immigration actions; First Amendment protection for noncitizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized that noncitizens have at least some First Amendment rights and that political speech is protected; the government may not implement Executive Orders or immigration actions in a viewpoint-discriminatory way to chill protected speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article discusses AAUP v. Rubio (Judge William G. Young) finding by 'clear and convincing evidence' that Secretaries Noem and Rubio and subordinates deliberately acted to chill speech, and later rulings that implemented remedies (stays on removals for certain plaintiffs, presumption of retribution for AAUP/MESA members, burden-shifting to the government to show non-retributive reasons). This establishes a legal standard limiting deportation/visa-revocation actions when motivated by viewpoint discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) review for executive immigration policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive actions and policies affecting immigration status are subject to review under the Administrative Procedure Act and can be set aside if unlawful under the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports that Judge Young declared the policy unlawful under the APA (January 2026), indicating that procedural and substantive administrative-law requirements constrain executive immigration policy. Implication: visa-revocation schemes and related executive orders can be invalidated if they do not comply with APA requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of minor infractions as pretextual grounds for revocation (reported practice/anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many visas were reported revoked based on minor violations such as speeding tickets, while only a small number cited national-security grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece treats this as an observed enforcement pattern suggesting pretextual use of minor infractions to justify revocations tied to political speech or protest. It is presented as an anti-pattern prompting legal challenges and restorations by courts in many instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on third-party lists/blacklists (e.g., Canary Mission) to identify targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Unsealed depositions revealed heavy reliance on the website Canary Mission and similar sources to identify pro‑Palestinian activists for deportation or visa revocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents this as an enforcement practice: use of external curated lists and online doxing as investigative sources. It raises questions about the reliability, transparency, and fairness of relying on such external compilations in immigration enforcement and was a central factual finding in litigation (AAUP v. Rubio).
